defect: The architecture changed mid-campaign and nothing recorded it (Act 4)
what it was: THE LARGEST ENTRY, and the one whose lesson generalises: A GOOD-LOOKING FIT IS NOT EVIDENCE OF A GOOD FIT. The cause of the ladder's architecture change is now known, and it is a PROCESS failure, not a hypothesis about position encodings that did not pan out and not a bug fix. src/scaling/ was EMPTY before commit f1eaf77. The ladder script committed in that commit builds ALiBiTransformer with 4 heads -- the SECOND family's architecture -- while its ASPECT_LADDER shape table is dim = 32 x layers (128/4, 160/5, 192/6, 224/7, 256/8, 288/9), which matches the canonical MiniGPT runs' shapes EXACTLY. The script that trained the canonical MiniGPT rungs was NEVER COMMITTED AT ALL. A training pipeline that was never in the repository made a mid-campaign change of model class invisible to every downstream artefact, including the ledger.
how it was caught: A PROVENANCE READ of the repository itself, on top of the provenance read of the run records that separated the two families. The two families coexist in one ladder because NOTHING recorded which script produced which points: the runs that carry an 'architecture' block are the ones re-run after f1eaf77 (or after 0932d19, which added the block), and the runs without one are the older ones. The ladder's shape table, the fit, the ledger and the figures all treated the pooled points as one model family. The repair is a CONFIG HASH computed from the LIVE model at the moment a point is logged, not retroactively from a rung table, because retroactive tagging is exactly what let the change hide in plain sight.
what it invalidated: The ladder's homogeneity, which was an assumption and never a measurement, and with it every artefact that pooled the two families: the fit, the figures and the ledger's own record. It is the reason the paper's generalised lesson is a procedure rather than an admonition: you need the points to be one model family, and the only way to know that is to tag every point with its configuration and check.

what it was: The input text never reached the prompt. The task builder passed the payload positionally, binding it to 'response' and leaving 'input_text' empty, so six of seven tasks were unanswerable by construction while still being scored.
how it was caught: A per-position accuracy profile: the first response token was unguessable (0.070) while positions 1-2 were trivially copyable from the true prefix (0.927 / 0.900), and the training loss was 0.3151, so the token distribution had been learned. That profile is diagnostic of a prompt that omits the input, not of a weak model.
what it invalidated: The whole first Act 7 result set (full fine-tuning 0.0104, every PEFT method 0.0000), which read exactly like a legitimate negative result. After the fix, the same recipe scores 0.6250.

what it was: A second cross-entropy shift in three PEFT forwards. MiniGPT computes the loss with no internal shift, but the prompt-tuning, prefix-tuning and adapter wrappers shifted a second time, and the response scorer sliced the logits off by one where a method prepends virtual tokens.
how it was caught: All three methods reported exactly 0.0000 while genuinely training, which is impossible for a method that is fitting; the off-by-one slice was then pinned by constructing the already-correct case.
what it invalidated: The prompt-tuning, prefix-tuning and adapter arms of 7c. LoRA and full fine-tuning route through the MiniGPT forward and were never affected, so 7b and 7d were correct the first time.

what it was: The held-out metric compared logits to the wrong position: each position was scored against the token at that position rather than the token one ahead of it.
how it was caught: An absolute sanity check: cross-entropy 11.98 nats (perplexity 1.6e5) for a model whose real held-out loss is about 2.5, which is 160,000 times worse than uniform over a 6,487-token vocabulary (ln 6487 = 8.78 nats). The uniform test alone cannot catch the shift, because it returns ln V either way; the next-token oracle is the test that does.
what it invalidated: Every Act 9 ablation delta. The metric is now pinned by a constructed next-token oracle (must score about 0) and a uniform model (must score exactly ln V).

what it was: Speculative decoding re-fed the whole sequence at the top of every round, on top of an already-prefilled KV cache, so the target's distribution p differed from the draft's q even when the two were the same weights.
how it was caught: An absolute invariant: acceptance must be exactly 100% at a zero draft-target gap, because p = q makes min(1, p/q) = 1 for every token. The cached-versus-uncached equivalence tests both PASSED, because both paths shared the bug and agreed with each other while both were wrong.
what it invalidated: Every 5c number taken before the fix: zero-gap acceptance 15.6% at K = 3 and 28.9 tokens/s. After the fix, acceptance is 100% and throughput is 309.8 tokens/s, a 10.7x improvement.

what it was: The conventional 4-shot ICL prompt was 328 tokens against a 128-token window, so truncation deleted the demonstrations before the model ever saw them.
how it was caught: A positive control that recorded the original prompt's token count and the number of visible shots ('2/4 (truncated away)'). The metric was sound; the prompt was not.
what it invalidated: The first ICL measurement, which reported 0.0000 and read as a negative result about in-context learning.

what it was: A flat 'chance = 1/3' baseline, which is wrong because the candidate set is deduplicated and heterogeneous: it holds 3, 4, 5 or 6 distinct numbers (1, 3, 8 and 28 items respectively).
how it was caught: Counting the candidates per item, which gives the per-item uniform chance of 0.1838 and forces every chance-adjusted rate to be computed per condition.
what it invalidated: The direction of the comparison. Against a false 1/3 baseline every condition looks below chance; against the true 0.1838 baseline every chance-adjusted rate is not significant.

what it was: The retriever was queried with the instruction text, whose terms (what, number, does, the, passage, state) cannot come from a passage about a number, so term-overlap ranking degenerated to a constant and the tie-break returned the SAME chunk for all 40 items.
how it was caught: Inspecting what the retriever actually returned: one distinct document for all 40 items, and the identical top chunk (score 0.6667) for two different failing items.
what it invalidated: The retrieved condition's earlier 0/40, which read like a finding. The retriever was working; it was being asked an impossible question. After the fix: 39 distinct documents, a 0.975 document hit rate, and a condition measured at 8/40, at chance.

what it was: The 'pe-alibi' arm ran the no-positional-encoding model, because the ALiBi positional-encoding module returns its input unchanged and the forward pass carries the comment 'ALiBi: apply attention bias (not implemented, skip)'.
how it was caught: The two rows differ by 4.8e-08 nats (2.4850885868 against 2.4850885391), which is float32 round-off, and the two loss trajectories agree to the same precision at every logged step. No real effect is that small.
what it invalidated: The claim that ALiBi is competitive with learned absolute positions. The honest reading of the table is that no positional encoding scored best among those actually implemented, and that ALiBi was not measured at all.

defect: Two architecture families in one ladder (Act 4)
what it was: THE LARGEST ENTRY, and the one whose lesson generalises: A GOOD-LOOKING FIT IS NOT EVIDENCE OF A GOOD FIT. At the time of the audit 11 of the 16 ladder runs were the canonical MiniGPT and 5 were a different family with no learned position table, and the tracked fit consumed points from both, so 51.4% of the fitted set came from a different model class. The fit was GOOD: R^2 = 0.9950 in sample, a plausible irreducible loss of 1.605 nats, plausible residuals, and a leave-one-rung-out headline of R^2 >= 0.985 on every held-out rung. It was fitting the wrong models. The other family occupied the ENTIRE TOP of the ladder (the 4.1M and 9.0M rungs) and two of the three runs at the 1.5M rung, so the fit's good looking was the other family's good looking.
how it was caught: Three things, and the first is the one that generalises. (i) An ABSOLUTE INVARIANT: the fit's own parameters score R^2 = +0.9957 on the other family's 1428 points, +0.2874 on the reconstructed mixed set, and R^2 = -0.6661 on the canonical models' own 3463 points. No fit of these models can score a negative R^2 on their own points, so that single number is a violation of an absolute, not a comparison. A residual plot could not have shown it: the mixed fit's residuals are still flat in log N and log D. (ii) A PROVENANCE READ of the run records, the surviving checkpoints' state dicts and the architecture block that the training code writes into every metrics.json, which is what identified WHICH runs were contaminated. The repair is a CONFIG HASH computed from the LIVE model at the moment a point is logged, not retroactively from a rung table, because retroactive tagging is exactly what let a mid-campaign architecture change hide in plain sight. (iii) A REPRODUCTION FROM THE REPOSITORY'S OWN CODE: the other family's 129.57-223.77 nat step-1 losses are an INITIALISATION property of that model class, not a metric bug and not divergence -- building that class with the repository's own seed on the same data reproduces 133.25 / 184.49 / 224.99 against the recorded 129.57 / 183.96 / 223.77, the metric is an average rather than a sum (a summed metric would be about 36,000 nats) and it is not misaligned (the canonical family's step-1 loss is 8.80 against a uniform-over-6,487-vocabulary cross-entropy of ln 6487 = 8.78). Those five runs were GOOD models that trained normally and finished at 3.578 nats at the 1.5M rung against the canonical 3.0468; they were invisible because their trajectory started 15-25x above uniform, so a plausible-looking curve sat at a plausible-looking N with a plausible-looking R^2 and nothing in the artefacts distinguished it.
what it invalidated: The centrepiece number. alpha = 0.445, beta = 0.290 and E = 1.605 are withdrawn; the leave-one-rung-out 'R^2 >= 0.985 on every rung' headline is withdrawn, because it was produced by the other family; and the comparison with Chinchilla that rested on that fit is withdrawn with it, and has to be re-established on the surviving fit under the correct parameter convention rather than assumed. What the refit is NOT is a minor correction: a reader who does not know that the other family owned the top of the ladder will read the refit as a small adjustment, and it is not one. The CAUSE of the contamination is now known too, and it is the entry above this one.

what it was: The ladder's recorded N was a NON-EMBEDDING parameter count, while the published exponents (Kaplan, Chinchilla) are fitted on TOTAL parameters. The two were therefore never on the same axis, and the confound was unstated: every comparison of our exponent with a published one was a comparison of two different quantities.
how it was caught: One ground that survives, and two that were withdrawn. (i) The convention is the PUBLISHED one: Kaplan and Chinchilla regress on total parameters, so the total axis is the only axis on which a comparison is like-for-like. This is the ground the paper still uses. (ii) It is the STABLE one: under total N the point estimate and the fold-wise mean agree (+0.589 against +0.587) -- but they now agree under non-embedding too (+0.407 against +0.407), so on the widened ladder stability no longer separates the two axes and the argument is RETIRED. (iii) An ABSOLUTE PLAUSIBILITY CHECK on the fitted irreducible loss, which put the two axes on opposite sides of what a next-token model can reach, was FALSIFIED BY MEASUREMENT and is withdrawn: the corpus's measured unigram entropy under the 6,487-token vocabulary is 4.9946 nats, BOTH fitted E values lie below it (1.964 is 0.39x it and 1.911 is 0.38x it), and against the 2.5152 nats the best model actually reaches the two axes are 0.78x and 0.76x. The physical-plausibility ground therefore does not discriminate.
what it invalidated: Every comparison of our exponents with a published value, in both directions. The result reverses: the profile likelihood's compatible alpha range is [0.34, 0.82] on the total-parameter axis and [0.20, 0.60] on the non-embedding axis, so the alpha comparison is compatible on both axes and discriminates between neither. The convention is now stated in the paper rather than left implied, and the paper reports one ground for it rather than three.

defect: Three N conventions in one table, none of them flagged (Act 4)
what it was: A per-rung audit of every N against three independent sources -- the ladder CSV's column, the run's own recorded metric, and the architecture the run implies -- finds that the table mixes three N conventions and flags none of them. Every row agrees except the 0.8M rung, whose recorded N of 694,144 matches NO MiniGPT or ALiBi shape at any (dim, layers, heads) in dims 16-256 and depths 1-10, while its embedding parameters (830,336 = 6,487 x 128) show the vocabulary and dim are as expected. The 0.8M rung is therefore a THIRD, unidentifiable architecture: it has no architecture block, it ran on CPU, it sits at D/N = 22.7 rather than 20, and it carries FOUR provenance stories (694,144 recorded, 809,728 the MiniGPT shape, 793,344 the other family's shape, 786,432 the LADDER design target).
how it was caught: AN EXACT INTEGER AUDIT against three independent sources, one of them a re-derivation rather than a quotation: the CSV column and the run's recorded metric are re-derived from the tracked ladder points and the tracked run records, and the architecture-implied and design-target columns are quoted from the project ledger. The 0.8M rung is then confirmed to be unidentifiable by a search over every (dim, layers, heads) in dims 16-256 and depths 1-10.
what it invalidated: The 0.8M rung's standing as a canonical model, and with it the worst hold-out fold in the act (R^2 = 0.508 non-embedding, 0.779 total), which is the only fold whose N falls outside the fitted range once it is removed. The audit cannot repair the rung -- only a re-run can -- and the re-run is in the rescue plan, which is in flight and unfinished, so no repair number is reported in the paper.

what it was: The report specification says Act 2 ran 20 runs and Act 3 ran 5 tokenizers.
how it was caught: Counting the runs in the tracked result files: 18 configurations in the Act 2 summary and 8 runs (4 tokenizer families x 2 controls) in the Act 3 summary.
what it invalidated: No measurement: both sweeps were correct, and the report's own text says 18 configurations and four tokenizer families. What it invalidated was the description of the sample, which is the first thing a reader checks.

what it was: The random-ablation null was measured against a stale baseline, because the head-ablation function did not record its own intact loss in the module-level slot the null reads.
how it was caught: A sanity check on the z-scores themselves: -88 instead of +42.8. A negative z of that size is a sign error, not a measurement.
what it invalidated: The random-ablation null itself, and therefore every z-score in the act. The fix is to record the baseline inside the head-ablation function.

what it was: The answer-copying score absorbed the prompt's own log-probability, because it summed over the whole sequence. Harmless within one prompt, invalid for every across-condition contrast, since the oracle prompt is far longer than the closed-book one.
how it was caught: An absolute plausibility check: a passage-lift of -246 nats, which is absurd on its face. The fix is pinned by a test with a constant-logit stub model, demonstrated failing against the old version (2 failures to 0).
what it invalidated: Every across-condition lift contrast in the first Act 8 write-up, and with them the interpretation of the passage-lift rows.
